articles.body: On Wednesday, Amazon unveiled five new Alexa devices: the Echo Show 16 ($499.99, pre-order), the Echo Studio with Home Camera ($249.99), a redesigned Echo Dot ($99.99), the Echo Time ($199.99), and the Alexa Photo Frame (from $199.99). The interesting part is the two cheapest new ideas in the list: a $200 clock and a $200 photo frame, in a year when your phone already does both for free. I read the announcements the way I always do — by asking what the product is actually selling, once you strip out the adjectives. What Amazon actually announced The Echo Dot is the workhorse of the lineup.

articles.title: Too many ADRs made our AI follow outdated decisions. The fix: keep them all, let an index name the current ones
articles.excerpt: The obvious fix for "my AI agent keeps relying on superseded architecture decisions" is a small parser: read each ADR's Supersedes field and mark the old records as replaced. We built exactly that. Th…
articles.body: The obvious fix for "my AI agent keeps relying on superseded architecture decisions" is a small parser: read each ADR's Supersedes field and mark the old records as replaced. We built exactly that. Then we ran it on two other repositories of ours, with 270 and 93 ADRs, and it reported live decisions as dead. In the larger repository, every one of the 5 records it called "superseded" was a false alarm. A parser that just picks up ADR numbers does not just miss things. It creates misreadings of its own, and an AI agent will trust them. This is a write-up of how we rebuilt the ADR index in ELN workflow, our in-house plugin suite for Claude Code, so that "which decisions are current?" is answered by one deterministic set of rules instead of by the model reading ADR bodies and guessing.
articles.author: uehara

articles.title: Notion Version History Is Just Timestamps. Here’s What Real Versioning Looks Like
articles.excerpt: I write technical documentation in Notion. A few weeks ago I needed to get back to “the version I sent to the client before the review” — a specific state I remembered clearly but couldn’t locate. I o…
articles.body: I write technical documentation in Notion. A few weeks ago I needed to get back to “the version I sent to the client before the review” — a specific state I remembered clearly but couldn’t locate. I opened Page History and got a flat list of timestamps. No labels, no summaries, no way to tell which snapshot was the one I wanted. I clicked through a dozen entries, comparing them by eye, and gave up. That was the moment I realized: Notion’s version history isn’t version control. It’s a list of timestamps. And for anyone who has used Git, that gap is hard to unsee. What Notion actually gives you Notion’s Page History records snapshots on a time interval . A new version is saved every 10 minutes while you’re actively editing or two minutes after you stop edit.

articles.title: AI Ban vs. Contribution Policy: What Open Source Maintainers Should Govern
articles.excerpt: A project maintainer opens a pull request and sees a patch that is plausible, poorly tested, and difficult to review. The contributor says an AI coding tool helped. What should happen next: reject the…
articles.body: A project maintainer opens a pull request and sees a patch that is plausible, poorly tested, and difficult to review. The contributor says an AI coding tool helped. What should happen next: reject the patch because AI was involved, ask for more evidence, or review it under the same quality bar as any other contribution? That question moved beyond code review on October 24, when moderators of Reddit's r/opensource announced that projects using AI, made with AI, or intended for AI would not be welcome. The same rule update added age, maintenance, contributor-count, and account-history requirements. It also rejected AI-translated submissions on the grounds that moderators could not reliably distinguish them from AI-written text.

articles.title: My forgotten subscriptions gave me nightmares, so I built Ghost Bills
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Picture this: it's the end of October, you open your bank app for something boring, and there it is. A…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Picture this: it's the end of October, you open your bank app for something boring, and there it is. A charge for $119 from a storage service you can't remember signing up for. It renews every November. It has renewed before. Nobody told you, because nobody was watching. That's a ghost. It lives in your statement, it takes a little money every month (or one big bite every year), and it's very good at staying invisible. So I built a ghost hunter. Ghost Bills reads your bank statement (a plain CSV export) and finds the subscriptions you forgot about. Then it tells you, in simple words, what each one costs you per year, and helps you get rid of it.

articles.title: How index keys affect inputs: compare DOM, row state, and parent state
articles.excerpt: When the first row is removed from a React list, do input values stay with the remaining rows? With index keys, the result depended on who owned the value. An uncontrolled input, whose value lived in…
articles.body: When the first row is removed from a React list, do input values stay with the remaining rows? With index keys, the result depended on who owned the value. An uncontrolled input, whose value lived in the DOM, and an input backed by row-local state displayed another row's value. Inputs receiving values from parent state displayed the correct values, but their DOM nodes were still reassigned to different rows. Narrow the reproduction from existing code The personal project's schedule creation screen passes the idx from rows.map as each Card key. It removes rows with array filtering and inserts duplicates by combining array slices. However, its title input is controlled through value={row.title} . The code alone does not show whether input values ever became mixed up in production.

articles.title: When “Send” Isn’t Risky: Context-Aware Confirmation in an Android AI Agent
articles.excerpt: When "Send" Isn't Risky: Context-Aware Confirmation in an Android AI Agent In the last post I covered the two-layer confirmation guard: the LLM's requires_confirmation flag plus a keyword guard as a d…
articles.body: When "Send" Isn't Risky: Context-Aware Confirmation in an Android AI Agent In the last post I covered the two-layer confirmation guard: the LLM's requires_confirmation flag plus a keyword guard as a dumb-but-reliable backstop. A reader raised the right follow-up: "send" in a banking app and "send" in a notes app are not the same risk. The guard shouldn't treat them the same way. This post covers the next layer — making the confirmation guard context-aware by weighing app identity and action type together. The Problem With a Flat Keyword List A flat list of risky keywords has two failure modes. False negatives (the dangerous kind): the guard misses a risky action because the label is in another language, uses a synonym, or comes from a resource ID the guard never sees.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.title: Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane
articles.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name. Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents. The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.
